name: Angel of the North
text: Your train passes near the Angel of the North, on the train's {side}, Antony Gormley's steel sculpture, 20 metres tall with wings 54 metres across. Completed in 1998 on the site of a former colliery, it is based on Gormley's own body, and an estimated 33 million people see it every year.

name: The Castle, Newcastle
text: Your train passes between the Castle Keep, on the train's {side}, and its gatehouse, the Black Gate. Henry II built the stone keep in 1172 to 1177 where the wooden 'New Castle' of 1080 had stood, and before that a Roman fort guarded a bridge over the Tyne here.

name: High Level Bridge, River Tyne
text: Your train crosses the Tyne on the High Level Bridge, designed by Robert Stephenson to link the railway towards Scotland. He added a road for vehicles and people on foot to bring in more money, and Queen Victoria opened the bridge in 1849.

name: St Peter's Church, Monkwearmouth
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church, Monkwearmouth, on the train's {side}, founded in 674 to 675 as one of the two churches of the monastery of Monkwearmouth and Jarrow. Bede wrote that its founder, Benedict Biscop, brought masons and glassworkers from Gaul, and the west wall and porch of his church still stand.

name: Seaham Hall
text: Your train passes near the country house, on the train's {side}, where the poet Lord Byron married Anne Isabella Milbanke in 1815. Their daughter was the mathematician Ada Lovelace, a pioneer of computing, and the house is now a hotel and spa.

name: Hawthorn Dene
text: Your train passes near Hawthorn Dene, on the train's {side}, a wooded valley that runs down to the railway. Its woodland of ash and wych elm grows on Magnesian Limestone, and yew grows on its lower slopes, which is rare in Britain.

name: HMS Trincomalee
text: Your train passes near HMS Trincomalee, on the train's {side}, a sailing frigate built of teak in Bombay and launched in 1817. She is the oldest British warship still afloat, and is now a museum ship at the National Museum of the Royal Navy.

name: PS Wingfield Castle
text: Your train passes near the paddle steamer Wingfield Castle, on the train's {side}, built locally and launched in 1934 as a ferry across the Humber. She was meant to become a floating restaurant at Swansea in the 1980s but was too wide for the lock gates, and is now a museum ship.

name: RAF Greatham
text: Your train passes near the site of RAF Greatham, on the train's {side}, little more than a grass airstrip in the Second World War. Four Spitfires of No. 403 Squadron, Royal Canadian Air Force, were based there from June 1942 to January 1943, and British Steel built on the site after the war.

name: St Mary's Church, Norton
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Norton, on the train's {side}, on the village green. Founded around 1020, it is the only cross-shaped Anglo-Saxon church in northern England, and is listed at Grade I.

name: Preston Hall, Preston-on-Tees
text: Your train passes near Preston Hall, on the train's {side}, a mansion built in 1825 and a museum since 1953. Its collection includes The Dice Players by the French painter Georges de La Tour.

name: Teesside High School
text: Your train passes near Teesside High School, on the train's {side}, formed in 1970 when the Cleveland School joined with Queen Victoria High School, founded in 1883. Its grounds were the Cleveland School's home, Woodside Hall on the banks of the Tees, from 1945.

name: Teesside Airport railway station
text: Your train runs through Teesside Airport station, on the original route of the Stockton and Darlington Railway. Opened in 1971, it was one of Britain's least-used stations, and its service has been suspended since May 2022, when its one working platform was condemned as unsafe.

name: St John's Church, Darlington
text: Your train passes near St John the Evangelist's Church, on the train's {side}, built in 1847 to 1849. Its foundation stone was laid by George Hudson MP, and a tall spire was planned for its tower but never built. It closed in 2023.

name: Durham Viaduct
text: Your train crosses a viaduct of eleven arches, 76 feet high, built in 1854 to 1857 and carrying the line over the city centre. From it there are views of the castle and cathedral, especially going north, as the railway comes out of a deep cutting.

name: Crook Hall, Durham
text: Your train passes near Crook Hall, on the train's {side}, whose oldest part is a hall of the 13th or 14th century, the only known domestic open hall in County Durham. It was extended in the 17th and 18th centuries, and its gardens are among the best in the north of England.

name: Skerne Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Skerne Bridge, built in 1825 for the Stockton and Darlington Railway and the oldest railway bridge in the world still in use. The engine Locomotion crossed it with the first train on September 27th 1825, and it appeared on the back of five-pound notes from 1990 to 2002.

name: Hopetown Carriage Works
text: Your train passes near Hopetown Carriage Works, on the train's {side}, built in 1853 by the Stockton and Darlington Railway. It made railway carriages until about 1884, when longer coaches came in, and it is now a museum workshop.

name: ROF Aycliffe
text: Your train passes near the site of a Royal Ordnance Factory, on the train's {side}, built in the early 1940s. About 17,000 women filled shells and bullets there, and they became known as the Aycliffe Angels after Lord Haw-Haw said in a Nazi propaganda broadcast that the little angels of Aycliffe would not get away with it.

name: Locomotion Museum
text: Your train passes Locomotion, the Science Museum Group's railway museum, on the train's {side}. Tony Blair opened it in 2004, and it was expected to draw 60,000 visitors a year, but had 94,000 in its first six months.

name: St Andrew's Church, South Church
text: Your train passes near St Andrew's Church, South Church, on the train's {side}, the largest church in County Durham. Built in the 13th century, it was once a collegiate church, and the astronomer Thomas Wright is buried in its churchyard.

name: Yarm Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the Tees, the boundary between County Durham and North Yorkshire, on a viaduct of 43 arches, two of stone over the river and the rest of red brick. It opened on May 15th 1852, and stands high above the town.

name: Stockton railway station (S&D)
text: Your train passes near the site of the Stockton and Darlington Railway's station in Stockton, on the train's {side}, opened on September 27th 1825. Its trains were drawn by horses at first, with steam from 1833, and its booking office still stands.

name: Tees Victoria Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Victoria Bridge, on the train's {side}, which carries the road over the Tees. It was built from 1882 to 1887 and named for Queen Victoria's 50 years on the throne, replacing a five-arch bridge of 1771.

name: Tees Newport Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Newport Bridge, on the train's {side}, the first large vertical-lift bridge in Britain. Opened in 1934, its 2,700-tonne road deck could be raised between two towers to let ships through, until its last lift in 1990.

name: Tees Transporter Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Transporter Bridge, on the train's {side}, the longest transporter bridge left in the world. Opened in 1911, it carries a gondola hung below its span across the Tees in 90 seconds, with room for 200 people or nine cars, though it has been closed since 2019.

name: Middlesbrough meteorite
text: Your train passes the spot, on the train's {side}, where a meteorite fell at 3.35pm on March 14th 1881, by a railway siding. Workmen only yards away heard a rushing sound and a thud, and it left a hole that a man's arm could be pushed into.

name: Captain Cook Birthplace Museum
text: Your train passes near the Captain Cook Birthplace Museum, on the train's {side}, in Stewart Park. It opened in 1978, 250 years after James Cook was born on the spot, and a granite urn put up in the 1850s by Henry Bolckow marks where the cottage stood.

name: Ormesby Hall
text: Your train passes near Ormesby Hall, on the train's {side}, a Palladian mansion finished in 1754 and home to the Pennyman family. The National Trust opened it in 1983, and it has a Victorian kitchen and a model railway.

name: Nunthorpe
text: Your train passes near the village, on the train's {side}, which was called Thorpe in the Domesday Book. Towards the end of the 12th century Cistercian nuns, said to have been thrown out of Hutton Lowcross for rowdy behaviour, settled there for a few years, and it has been Nunthorpe ever since.

name: Langbaurgh Ridge
text: Your train passes near Langbaurgh Ridge, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest for its rock. It exposes the Cleveland Dyke, an intrusion of once-molten rock linked to the ancient volcanic centre on the Isle of Mull in Scotland.

name: Teesside Steelworks
text: Your train passes the Teesside Steelworks, on the train's {side}, which stretched along the south bank of the Tees. Its blast furnace by the mouth of the river, opened in 1979, was the second largest in Europe, and closed in 2015.

name: Zetland (lifeboat)
text: Your train passes near the Zetland, on the train's {side}, the oldest lifeboat left in the world, stationed in the town in 1802. Her crew of 13 had oars painted blue and white, so the order could be to pull on the blues or back on the whites, and she is thought to have saved more than 500 lives.

name: Marske Aerodrome
text: Your train passes near the site of Marske Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, used by the Royal Flying Corps and the Royal Air Force from 1917 to 1920 to train pilots in air fighting. W. E. Johns, who wrote the Biggles books, did his training there.

name: Marske Hall
text: Your train passes near Marske Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1625 by William Pennyman. Its front of nine bays, with two turrets and the Pennyman arms, is little changed, and it is now a care home.

name: Saltburn Cliff Lift
text: Your train passes near the cliff lift, on the train's {side}, built in 1883 to 1884 to take people down to the pier. It is the oldest working water-balance cliff railway in the United Kingdom: water is added to or let out of a tank under each car to move them up and down.

name: Byker Wall
text: Your train passes near the Byker Wall, on the train's {side}, an unbroken block of 620 maisonettes designed by Ralph Erskine and built from 1969 to 1982. It replaced Victorian slums, and was designed to shield the estate from a motorway that was never built.

name: Ouseburn Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the Ouseburn Viaduct, 108 feet high over the valley of the Ouseburn. It was built in 1839 with timber arches for the Newcastle and North Shields Railway, and they were replaced with almost identical wrought iron spans 30 years later.

name: Cramlington Aerodrome
text: Your train passes near the site of an airfield, on the train's {side}, set up in 1915 to defend Tyneside against Zeppelin raids, the first Royal Flying Corps airfield in north-east England. It later served Tyneside as a civil airfield until 1935, when Newcastle's airport replaced it.

name: Morpeth Castle
text: Your train passes near what is left of a 14th-century castle, on the train's {side}, its gatehouse now a holiday home cared for by the Landmark Trust. Margaret Tudor, Henry VIII's sister, stayed there for four months in 1516 while fleeing her enemies in Scotland.
